meta.title: Transfer pricing and performance measurement
meta.summary: Management control systems, market-based, cost-based and negotiated transfer prices, the minimum transfer price rule, multinational taxes, ROI, residual income and EVA, and a recap of the course.

videos.title: Management control and transfer prices
videos.take: Transfer prices should promote goal congruence, effort and autonomy; methods are market, cost or negotiated

scenes.say: Tallgrass has grown into two divisions. Motors makes the electric drive units. Assembly builds the bikes. What should Assembly pay Motors?

sub: another for a product or service
scenes.say: A transfer price is the price one subunit of an organization charges another for a product or service. It's revenue for Motors and a cost for Assembly, so it drives both divisions' profits.

scenes.heading: What a good control system promotes
items: Goal congruence: managers act in the company's interest
scenes.say: A good management control system, including transfer prices, promotes goal congruence, so managers acting in their own interest also act in the company's; management effort; subunit autonomy; and fair performance evaluation.

scenes.heading: Three methods
scenes.say: There are three methods. Market-based prices use the outside price, best when there's a competitive market. Cost-based prices use variable or full cost, sometimes plus a markup, when no market price exists. Negotiated prices come from bargaining between the divisions.

scenes.heading: Motors division, per drive unit
rows: Selling cost saved on internal sale
scenes.say: Motors' variable cost is $180 per drive unit, full cost $260. Outside buyers pay $320. Selling internally saves $20 of selling cost.

scenes.q: When managers acting in their own interest also act in the company's interest, that's:
scenes.say: Quick check. When managers acting in their own interest also act in the company's interest, what's that called? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The minimum transfer price
videos.take: Minimum transfer price = incremental cost per unit + opportunity cost per unit

scenes.say: One rule tells you the lowest price the selling division should accept.
The minimum transfer price equals the incremental cost per unit up to the point of transfer, plus the opportunity cost per unit to the selling division.

scenes.heading: Does Motors have spare capacity?
scenes.say: With idle capacity, Motors gives up nothing, so the minimum is the $180 variable cost. At full capacity, every internal unit displaces an outside sale. Incremental cost is $160 after the $20 saving, plus $140 of lost margin, so the minimum is $300: the market price less the selling cost saved.
Assembly won't pay more than the $320 it would pay outside. With idle capacity, any price from $180 to $320 benefits the company. Where in that range it lands just divides the profit.

sub: even when Motors has idle capacity
scenes.say: Full-cost transfer prices can mislead. Fixed costs make units look more costly than they are, and divisions may make choices that hurt the company. Dual pricing, where the seller is credited at one price and the buyer charged another, is one fix.

scenes.q: Motors is at full capacity. The market price is $320 and $20 of selling cost is saved internally. Minimum transfer price?
scenes.say: Quick check. Motors is at full capacity. Market price three twenty; twenty dollars saved internally. Minimum transfer price? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Multinational transfer pricing and taxes
videos.take: Across borders, transfer prices shift taxable income; the arm's-length standard limits them

scenes.say: When divisions sit in different countries, the transfer price also decides where profit is taxed.

scenes.heading: Per 1,000 units, foreign tax rate 15%
scenes.say: Suppose Motors were in a country with a fifteen percent tax rate, and Assembly stayed in the US at twenty-one percent. Raising the transfer price by forty dollars on a thousand units shifts $40,000 of profit abroad. That saves $8,400 of US tax but costs $6,000 abroad. Net saving: $2,400.

Tax authorities don't let companies pick any price. Under the arm's-length standard, in the US Internal Revenue Code Section 482 and in OECD guidelines, related parties must price as unrelated parties would.

scenes.heading: Other factors
items: Limits on moving cash out of a country
Global minimum taxes on large groups
scenes.say: Other factors matter too: customs duties based on the import value, restrictions on moving cash out of some countries, global minimum tax rules for large groups, and how the local managers are evaluated and motivated.
One transfer price can't serve every purpose perfectly, so many multinationals keep one price for tax and a different measure internally for evaluating managers.

scenes.q: The rule that related parties must price as unrelated parties would is called:
scenes.say: Quick check. The rule that related parties must price as unrelated parties would is called what? Pause and pick.

videos.title: ROI, residual income and EVA
videos.take: ROI = income ÷ investment; RI = income − required return × investment; EVA uses after-tax income and WACC

scenes.say: How do you compare a division's profit with the money tied up in it? Three measures.

scenes.heading: Division results
scenes.say: Return on investment is operating income divided by investment. Motors earns $600,000 on $4 million of assets: fifteen percent. Assembly earns $900,000 on $7.5 million: twelve percent.

The DuPont method splits ROI into return on sales times investment turnover. Motors has $5 million of revenue: a twelve percent margin times a turnover of one point two five gives fifteen percent. Improve either to raise ROI.

scenes.heading: Residual income at 10% required return
scenes.say: Residual income is operating income minus the required rate of return times investment. Motors: $200,000. Assembly: $150,000. Both earn more than the ten percent required.

Economic value added is a version of residual income: after-tax operating income minus the weighted-average cost of capital times total assets less current liabilities. For Motors, $450,000 after tax, less nine percent of $3.5 million, gives $135,000.

scenes.q: Operating income $300,000; investment $2,000,000; required return 10%. Residual income?
scenes.say: Quick check. Operating income three hundred thousand; investment two million; required return ten percent. Residual income? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Choosing measures and the ROI trap
videos.take: ROI can make managers reject projects that beat the required return; RI and EVA don't

scenes.say: The measure you choose changes the decisions managers make.

scenes.heading: Motors considers a new project
scenes.say: Motors can invest $1 million in a project earning $130,000: thirteen percent, well above the ten percent required. But it would pull Motors' ROI down from fifteen to fourteen point six percent. A manager judged on ROI says no. Residual income rises by $30,000, so a manager judged on RI says yes.

scenes.big: RI and EVA promote goal congruence
scenes.say: That's why many firms prefer residual income or EVA: any project that beats the required return raises them.

scenes.heading: Other measurement choices
items: Time horizon: one year or several
Investment: total assets or net of liabilities
Asset value: net book, gross book or current cost
Target levels and timing of feedback
scenes.say: Other choices matter too: the time horizon; whether investment is total assets or net of current liabilities; whether assets are at net book value, which makes old plants look good, gross book value, or current cost; and the targets and timing of feedback.

Finally, reward managers for what they can control, balance incentive pay against the risk they bear, and use nonfinancial measures, like the balanced scorecard from Lecture 10, alongside the financial ones.

scenes.q: A division's ROI is 18%; required return is 12%. A project offers 15%. Who accepts it?
scenes.say: Quick check. A division's ROI is eighteen percent; required return twelve. A project offers fifteen percent. Who accepts it? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. ROI would fall, but RI rises.

videos.title: Course recap: Cost Accounting II
videos.take: Predict costs, plan, decide, then measure and control: the cost accountant's toolkit for management

scenes.say: Fourteen lectures in two minutes: how cost information helps managers plan, decide and control.

scenes.heading: Cost behavior and planning
items: Cost functions, regression and learning curves
scenes.say: First, cost behavior and planning: estimating cost functions with regression and learning curves, using data analytics to predict, cost-volume-profit analysis, and the master budget with responsibility accounting.

scenes.heading: Decisions
items: Relevant costs: make or buy, special orders
scenes.say: Then decisions: variable versus absorption costing and capacity, relevant costs for make-or-buy and special orders, pricing and target costing, and capital budgeting with NPV and IRR.

scenes.heading: Performance and control
items: Transfer prices, ROI, RI and EVA
scenes.say: And performance and control: cost allocation and customer profitability, strategy and the balanced scorecard, quality, time, inventory management and just-in-time, and transfer prices with ROI, residual income and EVA.

sub: Ask: what decision is this for?
scenes.say: The one idea tying it all together: different costs for different purposes. Before using any cost number, ask what decision it's for.

scenes.q: Which measure is best for ranking long-term investments?
scenes.say: Last quick check. Which measure is best for ranking long-term investments? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, net present value. Good luck on the final, and thanks for riding with Tallgrass.

warmup: Motors could sell every drive unit outside for $320. Assembly says it should pay full cost, $260. Who's right, and does it matter to Tallgrass as a whole?
Sets up the minimum transfer price and the difference between company-wide and divisional profit.
acts: Motors has idle capacity. An outside supplier offers Assembly drive units at $250. Should Tallgrass buy outside? What transfer price range works?
No: Tallgrass pays $250 vs $180 incremental. Any price from $180 to $250 makes both divisions better off.
Motors is at full capacity. Assembly's outside offer is $290. Should Assembly buy outside?
Yes: internal minimum $300 exceeds $290; buying outside lets Motors earn $140 margin, a $10 company gain.
Compute the tax effect of a $40 higher transfer price on 10,000 units with tax rates of 25% (buyer) and 10% (seller).
Shifts $400,000; saves 400,000 × 15% = $60,000, subject to arm's-length rules.
Assembly's revenue is $9,000,000. Break its 12% ROI into margin and turnover.
Assembly has a project: $500,000 investment, $60,000 operating income. Would a manager judged on ROI accept it? On RI at 10%?
Project ROI 12% = division ROI, so ROI stays 12% (indifferent); RI +$10,000: accept.
Motors' plant is old and nearly fully depreciated. Why might its 15% ROI overstate performance compared with Assembly?
Net book value shrinks the denominator; use gross book or current cost to compare.
case: Motors (full capacity) sells drive units outside at $320, with variable cost $180 and $20 of selling costs saved internally. Assembly can buy a comparable unit outside for $305. Motors demands $320; Assembly offers $260 (full cost). Ana Vang must settle the dispute and also choose between ROI and RI for the year-end bonus plan.
What is the minimum transfer price, and should the transfer happen at all?
What happens to Tallgrass if Ana imposes $260?
Recommend ROI or RI for bonuses and explain.

Minimum $300; Assembly's maximum $305: transfer is worthwhile, price between $300 and $305 (company gains $5/unit vs buying outside). Imposing $260 pays Motors $40 a unit less than it gives up by not selling outside, harming Motors' evaluation and autonomy. Policy: market-based, less savings, with negotiation within the range; arbitration if needed. Use RI (or EVA) with gross-book or current-cost assets to avoid the ROI trap, plus balanced scorecard measures.
exam: Explain the minimum transfer price rule and apply it to a division with and without idle capacity.
Incremental cost + opportunity cost. Idle: variable cost only. Full: incremental cost + lost contribution margin = market price − savings.
Division X: operating income $480,000; assets $3,000,000; required return 12%. A project costing $600,000 earns $84,000. Compute ROI and RI before and after, and explain the conflict.
Before ROI 16%, RI $120,000. Project ROI 14%. After ROI 564/3,600 = 15.7%; RI $132,000. ROI falls so an ROI-judged manager rejects a value-adding project; RI rises.

take: Transfer prices split profit and affect decisions
